claim: The UK Biobank dataset comprises over 3000 phenotypes spanning the functions of multiple organs and physiological systems.
source: To generate an inclusive, holistic model of human aging, we queried a large, well-annotated human database (the United Kingdom BioBank [UKBB]) comprising over 3000 phenotypes that together span the functions of multiple organs and physiological systems.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the UKBB dataset characteristics.

claim: The UK Biobank contains medical, environmental, and genetic data on approximately 500,000 British volunteers.
source: The UKBB's medical, environmental, and genetic data on ~500,000 British volunteers is a unique resource to investigate the biology of aging.
evidence: Direct statement about the size and composition of the UKBB dataset.

claim: UKBB participants are not a random cross section of society.
source: While participants of UKBB are not a random cross section of society (Abdellaoui et al., 2019; Haworth et al., 2019), this rich database nonetheless likely provides generalizable insights into human aging and disease (Hanlon et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The UKBB database likely provides generalizable insights into human aging and disease despite participant selection bias.
source: While participants of UKBB are not a random cross section of society (Abdellaoui et al., 2019; Haworth et al., 2019), this rich database nonetheless likely provides generalizable insights into human aging and disease (Hanlon et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Hanlon et al., 2022.

claim: The majority of published studies on genes influencing human aging focus on lifespan measures such as age at death or parents' age at death.
source: The majority of those studies (Ruby et al., 2018; Pilling et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2019) focus on lifespan (Joshi et al., 2017; Timmers et al., 2019; Timmers et al., 2022), e.g., age at death or parents' age at death, or analyze cohorts of people with exceptional lifespan (Bae et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2020), or the presence or absence of one or few age-associated diseases (Timmers et al., 2022; Timmers et al., 2020; Zenin et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Researchers have used blood DNA methylation patterns to build biological age prediction algorithms (clocks) to identify genes that influence aspects of human aging.
source: Additionally, researchers have used molecular traits, such as blood proteins (Coenen et al., 2023) or blood DNA methylation patterns, to build and analyze biological age prediction algorithms (clocks) to identify genes that influence aspects of human aging (Gibson et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2018; McCartney et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A biological clock has been built using 3D facial scans.
source: Biological age clocks derived from one or few physiological measures have also been constructed, such as a biological clock built using 3D facial scans (Xia et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Xia et al., 2020.

claim: A biological clock built using the gut microbiome was used to identify individuals who might be aging slower or faster than average.
source: Likewise, a biological clock built using the gut microbiome (Wilmanski et al., 2021) was used to identify individuals who might be aging slower or faster than average and suggest drugs that might influence gut health.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Wilmanski et al., 2021.

claim: Aging of separate organs has been investigated and linked to age-associated diseases and mortality.
source: Recently, aging of separate organs has been investigated and linked to age-associated diseases and mortality (Tian et al., 2023), and biological age has been estimated using AI methods (Qiu et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Systolic blood pressure increases with age.
source: Examples include systolic blood pressure (shown in Figure 1), which increases with age, and hand-grip strength (shown in Figure 1B), which decreases with age.
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the relationship.

claim: Hand-grip strength decreases with age.
source: Examples include systolic blood pressure (shown in Figure 1), which increases with age, and hand-grip strength (shown in Figure 1B), which decreases with age.
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the relationship.

claim: The model that best predicts age incorporates data reflecting the activity of most, if not all, the organs and physiological systems.
source: The fact that the model best predicted chronological age when it received input from a wide range of physiological systems underscores the global, systemic nature of the aging process.
evidence: Inference drawn from the model's performance with different input combinations.

claim: The physiological phenotypes were used to predict female age with a root mean square error of 4.8 years and R²~0.63.
source: We utilized the physiological phenotypes listed in Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 4 and the PLS modeling described above to predict female age with a root mean square error of 4.8 years, R2~0.63, and predict male age with a root mean square error of 5.1 years, R2~0.6.
evidence: Direct statement of model performance metrics from the analysis.

claim: The physiological phenotypes were used to predict male age with a root mean square error of 5.1 years and R²~0.6.
source: We utilized the physiological phenotypes listed in Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 4 and the PLS modeling described above to predict female age with a root mean square error of 4.8 years, R2~0.63, and predict male age with a root mean square error of 5.1 years, R2~0.6.
evidence: Direct statement of model performance metrics from the analysis.

claim: There is a significant correlation of residuals (R²~0.56, p<10⁻²⁵⁵) between two assessments for UKBB participants who were evaluated longitudinally with intervals of up to 12 years.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we observed a significant correlation of residuals between two assessments for a small number of UKBB participants who were evaluated longitudinally (twice) with intervals of up to 12 years (R2~0.56, p<10–255).
evidence: Statistical analysis of longitudinal data from UKBB participants.

claim: ∆Age carries no information about the person's actual chronological age, as it is equally distributed across zero at any age.
source: The ∆Age parameter carries no information about the person's actual chronological age, as it is equally distributed across zero at any age (Figure 3A).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 3A showing the distribution.

claim: In the UKBB dataset analyzed, 8883 males and 5668 females passed away within 5 years of their initial test-center attendance.
source: In the UKBB dataset that we analyzed, a small number of participants (8883 males and 5668 females, Figure 3B) passed away within 5 years of their initial test-center attendance.
evidence: Direct statement of mortality data from the UKBB dataset.

claim: Mortality rates in the UKBB dataset exponentially double every 7.7 years for both males and females.
source: The distribution of these deaths among UKBB participants has a typical 'Gompertzian' shape, with mortality rates exponentially doubling every 7.7 years for both males and females (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of mortality data showing Gompertzian pattern.

claim: The effect of 1 year of ∆Age on the mortality rate was almost identical to that of 1 year of chronological age.
source: Notably, the effect of 1 year of ∆Age on the mortality rate was almost identical to that of 1 year of chronological age.
evidence: Comparison of mortality effects between ∆Age and chronological age.

claim: Death data were not considered during the development of the model of biological age or derivation of ∆Age.
source: It is important to emphasize that death data were not considered during the development of the model of biological age or derivation of ∆Age, and that ∆Age does not exhibit any correlation with chronological age (as illustrated in Figure 3A).
evidence: Statement about the methodology used in model development.

claim: There is a robust correlation of ∆Age with the age at death of the participant's father (p-value=1.9*10⁻⁴³ for females and p-value=3.9*10⁻³¹ for males).
source: Remarkably, we observed a robust correlation of ∆Age with the age at death of the participant's father (p-value=1.9*10–43 for females and p-value=3.9*10–31 for males) and mother (p-value=1.1*10–68 for females and p-value=1.3*10–32 for males).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between ∆Age and parental lifespan.

claim: There is a robust correlation of ∆Age with the age at death of the participant's mother (p-value=1.1*10⁻⁶⁸ for females and p-value=1.3*10⁻³² for males).
source: Remarkably, we observed a robust correlation of ∆Age with the age at death of the participant's father (p-value=1.9*10–43 for females and p-value=3.9*10–31 for males) and mother (p-value=1.1*10–68 for females and p-value=1.3*10–32 for males).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between ∆Age and parental lifespan.

claim: Individuals predicted to be biologically younger had parents who lived longer.
source: Individuals predicted to be biologically younger had parents who lived longer.
evidence: Inference from the correlation analysis between ∆Age and parental lifespan.

claim: Previous studies have shown that the lifespans of parents and offspring are correlated.
source: Previous studies have reported that the lifespans of parents and offspring are correlated (Ruby et al., 2018; Milman and Barzilai, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Personal wealth is positively associated with human lifespan.
source: Previous studies have shown that personal wealth is positively associated with human lifespan (Chetty et al., 2016; Wang and Geng, 2019), whereas smoking and excessive drinking are negatively associated with lifespan.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Smoking and excessive drinking are negatively associated with lifespan.
source: Previous studies have shown that personal wealth is positively associated with human lifespan (Chetty et al., 2016; Wang and Geng, 2019), whereas smoking and excessive drinking are negatively associated with lifespan.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Heel bone density has a strong association with ∆Age (p-value ~10⁻¹¹).
source: For example, heel bone density (UKBB field #3148) and thalamus volume (UKBB field #25011) both had strong associations with ∆Age (p-values were ~10–11 and 10–10, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between heel bone density and ∆Age.

claim: Thalamus volume has a strong association with ∆Age (p-value ~10⁻¹⁰).
source: For example, heel bone density (UKBB field #3148) and thalamus volume (UKBB field #25011) both had strong associations with ∆Age (p-values were ~10–11 and 10–10, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between thalamus volume and ∆Age.

claim: Wealth was positively correlated with a more youthful ∆Age.
source: As predicted, wealth was positively correlated with a more youthful ∆Age.
evidence: Analysis of correlation between wealth indicators and ∆Age.

claim: Home location has a strong and significant correlation with ∆Age.
source: For instance, parameters such as 'home location' (UKBB field id# 20075), 'place of birth' (UKBB field id# 129), 'Townsend deprivation index' (UKBB field id# 189), and 'total income' have a strong and significant correlation with ∆Age (Supplementary file 5, Supplementary file 6, Supplementary file 7, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between socioeconomic factors and ∆Age.

claim: Smoking and exposure to smoke were positively correlated with an older ∆Age.
source: Additionally, smoking and exposure to smoke (UKBB field ids# 20161 and 20162) were positively correlated with an older ∆Age.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between smoking and ∆Age.

claim: The overall frequency of alcohol consumption did not have a significant correlation with ∆Age.
source: In our data, the overall frequency of alcohol consumption (numerous UKBB fields, like 20414) did not have a significant correlation with ∆Age; however, the alcohol type did.
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between alcohol consumption frequency and ∆Age.

claim: Consuming beer and hard cider was positively correlated with ∆Age.
source: Consuming beer and hard cider (UKBB field id# 1588) was positively correlated with ∆Age, whereas consuming Champagne and other white wines (UKBB field id# 4418) was negatively correlated.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between beer/cider consumption and ∆Age.

claim: Consuming Champagne and other white wines was negatively correlated with ∆Age.
source: Consuming beer and hard cider (UKBB field id# 1588) was positively correlated with ∆Age, whereas consuming Champagne and other white wines (UKBB field id# 4418) was negatively correlated.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between Champagne/white wine consumption and ∆Age.

claim: The level of education achieved (qualifications) was the single most significant non-biological parameter that correlated with ∆Age in both males and females (p-value<10⁻²⁰⁰).
source: The single most significant non-biological parameter that correlated with ∆Age in both males and females (p-value<10–200) was 'qualifications' or the level of education achieved (UKBB field id# 6138).
evidence: Statistical analysis identifying education as the strongest non-biological correlate.

claim: Each additional level of education was progressively associated with increased 'youthfulness'.
source: Each additional level of education was progressively associated with increased 'youthfulness' (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Analysis of the relationship between education levels and ∆Age shown in figures.

claim: The effect size of education (–1.51) was much greater than that of wealth (–0.81) or place of birth (–0.13).
source: Interestingly, the effect size of education (–1.51) was much greater than that of wealth (–0.81) or place of birth (–0.13).
evidence: Comparison of effect sizes from statistical analysis.

claim: The amount of TV watching was positively correlated with ∆Age in both males and females.
source: The amount of TV watching (UKBB filed# 1070) was positively correlated with ∆Age in both males and females, whereas time spent outdoors (UKBB filed# 1050) for males and DIY projects (UKBB filed# 2624) for females were correlated with younger ∆Age.
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between TV watching and ∆Age.

claim: Time spent outdoors for males was correlated with younger ∆Age.
source: The amount of TV watching (UKBB filed# 1070) was positively correlated with ∆Age in both males and females, whereas time spent outdoors (UKBB filed# 1050) for males and DIY projects (UKBB filed# 2624) for females were correlated with younger ∆Age.
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between outdoor time and ∆Age in males.

claim: DIY projects for females were correlated with younger ∆Age.
source: The amount of TV watching (UKBB filed# 1070) was positively correlated with ∆Age in both males and females, whereas time spent outdoors (UKBB filed# 1050) for males and DIY projects (UKBB filed# 2624) for females were correlated with younger ∆Age.
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between DIY projects and ∆Age in females.

claim: The frequency with which people play computer games was the second strongest behavioral trait associated with ∆Age.
source: Intriguingly, the second strongest behavioral trait that was associated with ∆Age was the 'frequency with which people play computer games'.
evidence: Ranking of behavioral traits by strength of association with ∆Age.

claim: Playing computer games associated with youthfulness with a size effect of –2.2 and p-value of 4*10⁻⁸.
source: Playing computer games associated with youthfulness (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), with a size effect of –2.2 and p-value of 4*10–8.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between computer gaming and ∆Age.

claim: The association between computer gaming and youthfulness was equally strong when age was factored out from the regression.
source: This association was equally strong if 'age' was factored out from the regression, indicating that generational changes in leisure activities do not explain this association.
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for age effects.

claim: The inflation factor in the GWAS analysis was λgc=1.2005 for males and λgc=1.2531 for females.
source: The inflation factor in our analysis was λgc=1.2005 for males and λgc = 1.2531 for females.
evidence: Statistical quality control metric from GWAS analysis.

claim: LD regression intercepts were 1.0213±0.0083 for males and 1.0285±0.0119 for females.
source: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) regression intercepts were 1.0213±0.0083 and 1.0285±0.0119 for males and females, respectively.
evidence: Statistical quality control metric from LD regression analysis.

claim: Using a threshold of 10⁻⁹, 9 loci associated with ∆Age were identified in males and 25 loci in females.
source: Using a stringent multiple testing correction for GWAS (Chen et al., 2021) with a threshold of 10–9, we identified 9 loci associated with ∆Age in males and 25 loci in females (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Results from GWAS analysis with specified statistical threshold.

claim: Four genetic loci associated with ∆Age were found in both sexes: the HLA locus at chr6:32,600,000; chr10:64,900,000 containing NRBF2, JMJD1C, and TATDN1P1 genes; chr19:45,413,233 containing APOE, TOMM40, and APOC genes; and chr20:23,613,000 containing the CST3 gene.
source: Four of these loci were found in both sexes. Specifically, these include the HLA locus, located at chr6:32,600,000; chr10:64,900,000, a locus that contains NRBF2, JMJD1C, and TATDN1P1 genes; chr19:45,413,233, a locus that contains APOE, TOMM40, and APOC genes; and chr20:23,613,000, a locus that contains the CST3 gene.
evidence: Results from GWAS analysis identifying shared genetic loci.

claim: APOE has previously been associated with human longevity.
source: Two of these loci, APOE (Schächter et al., 1994; Sebastiani et al., 2019) and HLA (Yang et al., 2017), have previously been associated with human longevity, which increases our confidence in the analysis.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HLA has previously been associated with human longevity.
source: Two of these loci, APOE (Schächter et al., 1994; Sebastiani et al., 2019) and HLA (Yang et al., 2017), have previously been associated with human longevity, which increases our confidence in the analysis.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The HNF1A locus is associated with diabetes.
source: For example, the HNF1A (hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 homeobox A) locus (top SNP - rs1169284, ∆Age association p-value=3.0*10–23) is associated with diabetes (Shepherd et al., 2009) and cancer (Abel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Shepherd et al., 2009.

claim: The HNF1A locus is associated with cancer.
source: For example, the HNF1A (hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 homeobox A) locus (top SNP - rs1169284, ∆Age association p-value=3.0*10–23) is associated with diabetes (Shepherd et al., 2009) and cancer (Abel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Abel et al., 2018.

claim: The APOE locus is associated with Alzheimer's disease and coronary heart disease.
source: The APOE (apolipoprotein E) locus (top SNP - rs7412, ∆Age association p-value=4.4*10–33) is associated with Alzheimer's disease and coronary heart disease (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: Total genetic heritability (H²) of ∆Age was approximately 11% (0.108±0.009) for females and approximately 10% (0.096±0.008) for males.
source: We found that total genetic heritability (H2) of ∆Age was ~11% (0.108±0.009) for females and ~10% (0.096±0.008) for males, which is similar to the genetic heritability estimated previously for human longevity (Ruby et al., 2018; Melzer et al., 2020).
evidence: Results from LD score regression analysis.

claim: The genetic heritability of ∆Age is similar to the genetic heritability estimated previously for human longevity.
source: We found that total genetic heritability (H2) of ∆Age was ~11% (0.108±0.009) for females and ~10% (0.096±0.008) for males, which is similar to the genetic heritability estimated previously for human longevity (Ruby et al., 2018; Melzer et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with previous research supported by citations.

claim: GWAS of forced vital capacity (FVC) had a correlation with ∆Age GWAS of 0.49±0.02 (p-value=5*10⁻⁶⁵).
source: For example, GWAS of forced vital capacity (FVC) had a correlation with ∆Age GWAS of 0.49±0.02 (p-value=5*10–65).
evidence: Statistical comparison of GWAS signatures.

claim: GWAS signatures of blood creatinine levels had no genetic correlation with ∆Age (0.1±0.07, p-value=0.1).
source: In contrast, GWAS signatures of certain physiological parameters, such as blood creatinine levels, which were explicitly used in ∆Age derivation, had no genetic correlation with ∆Age (0.1±0.07, p-value=0.1).
evidence: Statistical comparison of GWAS signatures.

claim: The genetic correlation of GWAS for parent's age mortality with GWAS for offspring's ∆Age was 0.39±0.03, p-value=1*10⁻⁷ for females and 0.2±0.05, p-value=3*10⁻⁵ for males.
source: The genetic correlation of GWAS for parent's age mortality with GWAS for offspring's ∆Age was 0.39±0.03, p-value=1*10–7 for females and 0.2±0.05, p-value=3*10–5 for males.
evidence: Statistical comparison of GWAS signatures between parental mortality and offspring ∆Age.

claim: The top enriched gene ontology category (GO:98815) was modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential, enriched approximately 18-fold over the expected by-chance reference, with a multiple-testing-adjusted p-value of 0.046.
source: Unexpectedly, the top enriched category (GO:98815) was modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential, enriched ~18-fold over the expected by-chance reference, with a multiple-testing-adjusted p-value of 0.046.
evidence: Results from gene ontology analysis of GWAS hits.

claim: The nervous system plays a particularly important role in aging systemically.
source: This GO category comprised multiple genes influencing synaptic function (Table 1), suggesting that the nervous system plays a particularly important role in aging systemically.
evidence: Inference from gene ontology analysis results.

claim: CST3 had the most significant association with ∆Age (effect size>0.4, p-value<10⁻⁸⁰) in both males and females in the full model.
source: In the full model, CST3 had the most significant association with ∆Age (effect size>0.4, p-value<10–80) in both males and females, as represented by its large red bubble.
evidence: Results from GWAS analysis in the full model.

claim: When kidney clusters were omitted from the model, the size effect of the CST3 association decreased to less than 0.1, p-value~0.1.
source: When the kidney clusters were omitted, the size effect of the CST3 association decreased to less than 0.1, p-value~0.1, which is represented by the small black bubble.
evidence: Results from cluster-dropout analysis.

claim: Cystatin-C is a marker rather than a driver or determinant of aging.
source: Combined, these data suggest that cystatin-C is a 'marker' rather than a driver or determinant of aging.
evidence: Inference from cluster-dropout analysis results.

claim: The correlation between biological age and computer gaming remained significant across all the dropout models tested in both males and females.
source: The correlation between biological age and computer gaming remained significant across all the models tested in both males and females, suggesting that there are no specific singular phenotypes responsible for this correlation.
evidence: Results from cluster-dropout analysis of environmental factors.

claim: Particulate air pollution (pm10) is associated with older biological age (p-value=1.6*10⁻⁹ for females).
source: For example, particulate air pollution (pm10) is associated with older biological age (p-value=1.6*10–9 for females); however, if the model omits the cluster containing lung parameters, such as FEV, the correlation drops below Bonferroni-corrected statistical significance (p-value=5*10–3 for females).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation between air pollution and ∆Age.

claim: If the model omits the cluster containing lung parameters, the correlation between particulate air pollution and biological age drops below Bonferroni-corrected statistical significance (p-value=5*10⁻³ for females).
source: For example, particulate air pollution (pm10) is associated with older biological age (p-value=1.6*10–9 for females); however, if the model omits the cluster containing lung parameters, such as FEV, the correlation drops below Bonferroni-corrected statistical significance (p-value=5*10–3 for females).
evidence: Results from cluster-dropout analysis.

claim: Particulate pollution mostly affects pulmonary health and, to a lesser extent, global organismal aging.
source: This might suggest that particulate pollution mostly affects pulmonary health and, to a lesser extent, global organismal aging.
evidence: Inference from cluster-dropout analysis results.

claim: The study used a cross-sectional dataset where different ages are represented by people born at different times.
source: We used a cross-sectional dataset, where different ages are presented by people born at different times.
evidence: Description of the study design and its limitations.

claim: The model assumes that the rate of aging is constant for each individual.
source: Additionally, our model assumes that the rate of aging is constant for each individual, which is not always true.
evidence: Statement about a modeling assumption.

claim: Approximately 13,000 out of ~500,000 UKBB participants have been assessed twice, with follow-up intervals ranging from 4 to 12 years.
source: The robustness of our modeling can also be assessed by considering a small number of UKBB participants (~13,000 out of ~500,000), who have been assessed twice, with the follow-up intervals ranging from 4 to 12 years.
evidence: Description of longitudinal data available in UKBB.

claim: There is a significant correlation (R²~0.6, p-value<10⁻²⁵⁵) between biological-chronological age measures for individuals assessed twice.
source: We observed a significant correlation (R2~0.6, p-value<10–255) between biological-chronological age measures for these individuals between their two assessments.
evidence: Statistical analysis of longitudinal data.

claim: At all ages, even as young as 40 years, APOE genotype influences ∆Age.
source: However, we find that at all ages, even as young as 40 years, APOE genotype influences ∆Age (Figure 4F), perhaps due to its more general effects on lipid homeostasis (Abondio et al., 2019) or inflammation.
evidence: Analysis of APOE effects across age groups shown in Figure 4F.

claim: APOE's influence on ∆Age may be due to its effects on lipid homeostasis or inflammation.
source: However, we find that at all ages, even as young as 40 years, APOE genotype influences ∆Age (Figure 4F), perhaps due to its more general effects on lipid homeostasis (Abondio et al., 2019) or inflammation.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism supported by citation.

claim: There is no overlap between GWAS results for clocks built via different modalities (retina, DNA methylation, or physiological functions).
source: Surprisingly, we discovered that there is no overlap between GWAS results for any two of these clocks built via different modalities - retina, DNA methylation, or physiological functions.
evidence: Comparison of GWAS results across different aging clock modalities.

claim: There is a significant genetic overlap between clocks built using human phenotypic measures and the ∆Age model.
source: However, there is a significant genetic overlap between clocks built using human phenotypic measures and our ∆Age model we describe.
evidence: Comparison of GWAS results between phenotypic clocks.

claim: The Biological Age Clock Acceleration calculated using HbA1c, albumin, cholesterol, FEV, urea nitrogen, SBP, and creatinine yielded 16 significant hits in GWAS analysis, 5 of which were also significant in the GWAS for UKBB-based ∆Age.
source: For example, the Biological Age Clock Acceleration calculated using HbA1c, albumin, cholesterol, FEV, urea nitrogen, SBP, and creatinine (Levine, 2013) in a US cohort (from National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [NHANES]) yielded 16 significant hits in the GWAS analysis, 5 of which were also significant in our GWAS for UKBB-based ∆Age.
evidence: Comparison of GWAS results between different cohorts.

claim: The five common loci between the NHANES biological age clock and UKBB ∆Age were close to the following genes: APOB, PIK3CG, TRIB1, SMARCA4, and APOE.
source: These five common loci were close to the following genes: APOB, PIK3CG, TRIB1, SMARCA4, and APOE.
evidence: Identification of shared genetic loci between studies.

claim: The significance of the overlap between NHANES and UKBB GWAS results is p<10⁻⁸.
source: The significance of this overlap is p<10–8, suggesting that the ∆Age model we propose might be translatable to other cohorts of people.
evidence: Statistical assessment of the significance of GWAS overlap.

claim: Only 9-11 axes are necessary to predict age using PLS modeling.
source: When analyzing the many phenotypes that predict aging using PLS modeling, we discovered that only 9–11 axes are necessary to predict age.
evidence: Results from PLS modeling analysis.

claim: There might be only approximately 10 independent systems (physiological networks) driving human aging.
source: This suggests that there might be only ~10 independent systems (physiological networks) driving human aging.
evidence: Inference from the number of PLS components required.

claim: The two most valuable phenotypes used in the study were FVC and blood pressure.
source: That said, the two most valuable phenotypes used in our study (those that had, overall, the most weight in age prediction) were FVC and blood pressure.
evidence: Analysis of phenotype weights in the prediction model.

claim: The genetic signature of ∆Age was similar to the genetic signature for FVC and blood pressure.
source: Moreover, the genetic signature of ∆Age was similar to the genetic signature for FVC and blood pressure (Figure 4E).
evidence: Comparison of GWAS signatures shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The three approaches used to generate age prediction model (PLS, GBM, and linear regression) yielded very similar or identical results in performance.
source: It is interesting to note that the three approaches we used to generate age prediction model (PLS, GBM, and linear regression) yielded very similar or identical results in performance.
evidence: Comparison of different modeling approaches.

claim: The top genetic loci associations obtained via the PLS model were also obtained in the GBM and linear models.
source: Specifically, the top candidates (CST3, APOE, HLA locus, CPS1, PIK3CG, IGF1) identified in the PLS approach had statistically significant associations in all the models of ∆Age.
evidence: Validation of genetic findings across different modeling approaches.

claim: Measuring human biological age using 12 simple but diverse physiological measurements captures approximately 87% of the full ∆Age model.
source: Finally, from a practical perspective, we suggest that measuring human biological age using the 12 simple but diverse physiological measurements that together capture ~87% of the full ∆Age model (systolic blood pressure, FEV, and so forth; see Figure 2) might have actuarial and clinical value.
evidence: Analysis of model performance with reduced phenotype set.

claim: Over 60,000 participants (~15%) in the selected UKBB dataset lacked at least one phenotypic measurement.
source: Since PLS modeling and many other mathematical approaches do not tolerate missing values, and in the UKBB dataset that we selected, over 60,000 participants (~15%) lacked at least one measurement for one of the phenotypes, the following mitigation strategies had been used.
evidence: Description of data quality issues in the dataset.

claim: Any individual missing more than 15 data points was excluded from the study.
source: To avoid excessive imputation, any individual missing more than 15 data points was excluded from the study.
evidence: Description of data exclusion criteria.

claim: The number of selected female participants decreased from 222,111 to 215,949 (~2.7% loss) after excluding individuals with too many missing data points.
source: In females, the number of selected participants decreased from 222,111 to 215,949 (~2.7% loss), and in males from 188,609 to 183,715 (~2.6% loss).
evidence: Description of the impact of data exclusion on sample size.

claim: The number of selected male participants decreased from 188,609 to 183,715 (~2.6% loss) after excluding individuals with too many missing data points.
source: In females, the number of selected participants decreased from 222,111 to 215,949 (~2.7% loss), and in males from 188,609 to 183,715 (~2.6% loss).
evidence: Description of the impact of data exclusion on sample size.

claim: Only 11 independent components were required to describe female aging dynamics.
source: Our analysis revealed that only 11 independent components were required to describe female aging dynamics, and 9 independent components were required for males.
evidence: Results from PLS component selection analysis.

claim: Only 9 independent components were required to describe male aging dynamics.
source: Our analysis revealed that only 11 independent components were required to describe female aging dynamics, and 9 independent components were required for males.
evidence: Results from PLS component selection analysis.

claim: The effect of each year of physiological ∆Age on Gompertz mortality risk was equivalent to that of one chronological year.
source: Remarkably, the effect of each year of physiological ∆Age on Gompertz mortality risk was equivalent to that of one chronological year.
evidence: Analysis of mortality risk in relation to ∆Age and chronological age.

claim: People predicted to be young for their age had a lower subsequent mortality rate.
source: Differences between calculated 'biological' age and chronological age (∆Age) appear to reflect an individual's relative youthfulness, as people predicted to be young for their age had a lower subsequent mortality rate and a higher parental age at death, even though no mortality data were used to calculate ∆Age.
evidence: Analysis of mortality outcomes in relation to ∆Age.

claim: People predicted to be young for their age had a higher parental age at death.
source: Differences between calculated 'biological' age and chronological age (∆Age) appear to reflect an individual's relative youthfulness, as people predicted to be young for their age had a lower subsequent mortality rate and a higher parental age at death, even though no mortality data were used to calculate ∆Age.
evidence: Analysis of parental longevity in relation to offspring ∆Age.

claim: No mortality data were used to calculate ∆Age.
source: Differences between calculated 'biological' age and chronological age (∆Age) appear to reflect an individual's relative youthfulness, as people predicted to be young for their age had a lower subsequent mortality rate and a higher parental age at death, even though no mortality data were used to calculate ∆Age.
evidence: Description of the methodology used to calculate ∆Age.

claim: A GWAS of ∆Age identified known as well as new factors that may influence human aging.
source: A genome-wide association study (GWAS) of ∆Age and analysis of environmental factors associated with ∆Age identified known as well as new factors that may influence human aging, including genes involved in synapse biology and a tendency to play computer games.
evidence: Summary of GWAS findings.

claim: Genes involved in synapse biology may influence human aging.
source: A genome-wide association study (GWAS) of ∆Age and analysis of environmental factors associated with ∆Age identified known as well as new factors that may influence human aging, including genes involved in synapse biology and a tendency to play computer games.
evidence: Results from GWAS and gene ontology analysis.

claim: A tendency to play computer games may influence human aging.
source: A genome-wide association study (GWAS) of ∆Age and analysis of environmental factors associated with ∆Age identified known as well as new factors that may influence human aging, including genes involved in synapse biology and a tendency to play computer games.
evidence: Results from environmental factor analysis.

claim: The rate of aging has both genetic and environmental determinants.
source: The rate of aging, i.e., the rate at which organisms lose physiological fitness and accumulate morbidity, has both genetic and environmental determinants.
evidence: General statement about aging biology supported by the study design.

claim: Humans age more slowly than dogs.
source: Humans age more slowly than, for example, dogs, so genes play a key role, but environmental factors like smoking and exercise influence aging as well.
evidence: Comparative statement about aging rates across species.

claim: Environmental factors like smoking and exercise influence aging.
source: Humans age more slowly than, for example, dogs, so genes play a key role, but environmental factors like smoking and exercise influence aging as well.
evidence: General statement about environmental influences on aging.

claim: Most or all physiological systems (lung, heart, brain, etc.) contribute to the global phenotype of chronological age.
source: The model predicted a person's age with best accuracy when it heavily weighted traits that together query multiple organ systems, arguing that most or all physiological systems (lung, heart, brain, etc.) contribute to the global phenotype of chronological age.
evidence: Inference from model performance with different trait combinations.

claim: The outcomes of PLS and linear regression were almost identical (R-squared between ∆Age values derived by these two methods was 0.99).
source: The outcomes of PLS and linear regression were almost identical (R-squared between ∆Age values derived by these two methods was 0.99, meaning that if one model were to predict an individual was 62 years of age, the other model would have the same prediction).
evidence: Comparison of different modeling approaches.

claim: The correlation between GBM model outcomes and PLS was R-squared=0.87.
source: The correlation between GBM model outcomes and PLS (and linear regression) was slightly smaller (R-squared=0.87).
evidence: Comparison of GBM with PLS modeling approach.

claim: The reason for the lower correlation between GBM and PLS is likely the need for imputation in PLS and linear regression models.
source: The reason for the lower correlation is likely the need for imputation in PLS and linear regression models.
evidence: Explanation for differences in model performance.

claim: The GBM model tolerates missing data, whereas linear regression and PLS methods require imputation or removal of individuals with too many data points missing.
source: The GBM model tolerates missing data, whereas linear regression and PLS methods require imputation or removal of individuals with too many data points missing, an approach we describe in more detail below.
evidence: Description of methodological differences between modeling approaches.

claim: Most of the clusters appeared to be enriched for phenotypes associated with a specific organ or physiological system.
source: Notably, most of the clusters appeared to be enriched for phenotypes associated with a specific organ or physiological system.
evidence: Observation from cluster analysis of phenotypes.

claim: The cluster containing 'creatinine', 'urea', 'cystatin-C', and 'phosphate' likely reflects kidney function.
source: For example, the cluster that contains 'creatinine', 'urea', 'cystatin-C', and 'phosphate' likely reflects kidney function, whereas the cluster that contains 'systolic blood pressure' and 'diastolic blood pressure' likely reflects cardiovascular function (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Interpretation of phenotype clustering based on biological knowledge.

claim: The cluster containing 'systolic blood pressure' and 'diastolic blood pressure' likely reflects cardiovascular function.
source: For example, the cluster that contains 'creatinine', 'urea', 'cystatin-C', and 'phosphate' likely reflects kidney function, whereas the cluster that contains 'systolic blood pressure' and 'diastolic blood pressure' likely reflects cardiovascular function (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Interpretation of phenotype clustering based on biological knowledge.

claim: Elevated levels of cystatin-C have been linked to elevated risk of cardiovascular disease.
source: Elevated levels of this metabolite had been linked to elevated risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) (van der Laan et al., 2016), risk of cancer (Jones et al., 2017), and neurodegeneration (Kaur and Levy, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated levels of cystatin-C have been linked to risk of cancer.
source: Elevated levels of this metabolite had been linked to elevated risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) (van der Laan et al., 2016), risk of cancer (Jones et al., 2017), and neurodegeneration (Kaur and Levy, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated levels of cystatin-C have been linked to neurodegeneration.
source: Elevated levels of this metabolite had been linked to elevated risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) (van der Laan et al., 2016), risk of cancer (Jones et al., 2017), and neurodegeneration (Kaur and Levy, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In a Mendelian randomization study, while levels of cystatin-C predict CVD well, SNPs that robustly alter expression of cystatin-C do not associate with CVD.
source: However, in a Mendelian randomization study (van der Laan et al., 2016), it was shown that while levels of cystatin-C predict CVD well, SNPs that robustly alter expression of cystatin-C do not associate with CVD.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Mendelian randomization study.

claim: Cystatin-C concentration is one of the UKBB phenotypes used to generate the model.
source: This association remained significant in all the dropout models, except dropout number 3 (kidney health clusters), which contains the CST gene product, cystatin-C concentration, which was one of the UKBB phenotypes used to generate the model.
evidence: Description of phenotypes included in the model.

claim: If ∆Age is calculated using all the inputs in the full model except for 'cystatin-C levels', the CST3 locus is no longer associated with ∆Age.
source: Likewise, if we calculated ∆Age using all the inputs in the full model except for 'cystatin-C levels', the CST3 locus was no longer associated with ∆Age.
evidence: Results from sensitivity analysis excluding specific phenotypes.

claim: APOE4 individuals generally die prematurely of Alzheimer's disease.
source: One could imagine that this is the case for APOE, since APOE4 individuals generally die prematurely of Alzheimer's disease (Olichney et al., 1997; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Biological Age Clock Acceleration was calculated using HbA1c, albumin, cholesterol, FEV, urea nitrogen, SBP, and creatinine in a US cohort from NHANES.
source: For example, the Biological Age Clock Acceleration calculated using HbA1c, albumin, cholesterol, FEV, urea nitrogen, SBP, and creatinine (Levine, 2013) in a US cohort (from National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [NHANES]) yielded 16 significant hits in the GWAS analysis, 5 of which were also significant in our GWAS for UKBB-based ∆Age.
evidence: Description of another biological age clock from previous research.
